hints: Focus on the type of pathogen - TB is not caused by a virus, it is caused by a slow-growing bacterium with a waxy wall that is inhaled into the lungs.
walkthrough:
Remembering the TB bacterium**
TB is a bacterial infectious disease spread by droplets. The bacterium has a lipid-rich waxy cell wall so it survives inside lung macrophages. Its full binomial name is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with Mycobacterium as the genus with a capital M and tuberculosis as the species in lower case. Mycobacterium bovis is also accepted as it causes a very similar TB disease.
Final answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (accept Mycobacterium bovis). Spelling must be correct.

hints: Start by sorting the two lines - solid line is deaths, dashed line is new cases - and mark 1940 for antibiotics and 1948 for vaccine on the year axis.
Follow the solid deaths line from 1925 to 1950 - what was it doing before 1940 at about 50 to 80 per 100000, and when does the steep fall begin?
Now follow the dashed new cases line around 1940 to 1950 - does it fall straight away or does it level off and even rise to a peak near 100 to 104 per 100000?
Look at the long-term change after about 1950 to 2010 for both lines - what are the final values and what happens to deaths after 1948 from about 36 to 40 per 100000?
Think biologically about the difference - how does killing bacteria in a sick person differ from immunising healthy people to stop spread?
walkthrough:
Separating deaths from new cases**
The solid line shows people dying of TB, the dashed line shows people catching TB. They tell you different things. Antibiotics like streptomycin kill bacteria inside a person who is already ill, so you expect deaths to fall first. A vaccine makes healthy people immune before they meet the pathogen, so you expect new cases to fall by reduced transmission.

Effect of antibiotics from 1940**
Before 1940 deaths were high and fairly flat, around 50 to 80 per 100000. They do not fall immediately in 1940 but stay near 52 per 100000 until about 1943 to 1946, probably because the drug was not yet in widespread use. Then deaths fall steeply to about 25 per 100000 by 1951 and eventually to zero by about 1980. New cases do not fall either. They plateau at about 88 to 90 per 100000 from 1940 to 1944, then actually rise to a peak of about 100 to 104 per 100000 in 1946 to 1950 before falling. So antibiotics alone did not at first stop spread.

Effect of vaccine from 1948**
In 1948 deaths were about 36 to 40 per 100000. After 1948 the deaths line just keeps falling with the same trend, so the vaccine does not create a new sharp drop in deaths. New cases stay at about 100 per 100000 until about 1950, a short plateau, then fall continuously for decades to about 4 per 100000 in 2010. That delayed then sustained fall fits vaccination.

Linking to biology**
Antibiotics cure, so fewer infected people die. Vaccine gives active immunity with memory cells and antibody, so fewer susceptible people become infected. As more people are immunised, herd immunity builds up and transmission chains break, but that takes a few years, which explains the plateau to 1950 before the steady fall in new cases.

Final answer: After antibiotics from 1940: deaths stayed relatively constant at approx. 52 per 100000 until 1943-1946 then decreased sharply to zero by approx. 1980. New cases stopped increasing / plateaued at 88-90 per 100000, then increased to a peak of approx. 104 per 100000 in 1946 before decreasing. After vaccine from 1948: deaths continued to decrease with no change in trend, from 36-40 per 100000 in 1948. New cases plateaued briefly at approx. 100 per 100000 until 1950 then decreased steadily to approx. 4 per 100000 by 2010.

hints: Compare the two numbers in Table 3.1 - 400 deaths per 100000 in HIV+ versus 91 in HIV- - so HIV+ people are more than four times more likely to die of TB.
Recall which cells HIV infects and destroys, and what that means for the ability to mount a specific immune response with lymphocytes and phagocytes.
Link a weak immune system to TB control - think about keeping latent TB walled off in the lungs versus it becoming active, and fighting a new TB infection.
walkthrough:
What HIV does to immunity**
HIV infects and destroys helper T lymphocytes, which coordinate both humoral and cell-mediated immunity. Without enough helper T cells, B cell antibody production and activation of cytotoxic T cells and macrophages are weak. Many HIV+ people progress to AIDS with severe immunodeficiency.

Why TB then kills more**
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is normally held in check by T cells and macrophages forming granulomas in the lungs, often as latent TB. With weak immunity, the bacteria are not contained. Latent TB reactivates to active lung disease and new infections are not cleared. TB therefore acts as an opportunistic infection.

Reading Table 3.1**
That is why 400 per 100000 HIV+ people die of TB compared with only 91 per 100000 HIV- people. It is not just more cases, it is a greater chance of dying once infected, plus poorer response to treatment when the immune system cannot help.

Final answer: HIV develops to AIDS and weakens the immune system / immune response. TB is an opportunistic disease to which HIV+ people are more susceptible / latent TB is more likely to become active, so a greater proportion die of TB if HIV+.
